It sets itself apart from general illumination models by operating directly in the HSV color space to decouple brightness from hue and saturation, allowing for painterly effects where facing surfaces remain bright and edge-on surfaces fade [S1].

The claim states that the system operates in HSV color space to decouple brightness (value) from hue and saturation, allowing for painterly effects where facing surfaces remain bright and edge-on surfaces fade. The evidence explicitly states that the use of the HSV color space allows for intuitive color modification techniques of painters. It further confirms that the color value (V) is decreased as the angle between the gradient and the viewer increases, which simulates oriented fading. In volume rendering, a gradient vector pointing towards the viewer corresponds to a 'facing' surface (angle is small), while a gradient vector perpendicular to the viewer corresponds to an 'edge-on' surface (angle is large). Therefore, decreasing value as the angle increases means facing surfaces (small angle) retain higher value (brightness) and edge-on surfaces (large angle) fade (lower value). This aligns perfectly with the claim.
